Town of Alta Annex
To participate in this multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan (MJHMP) update for Salt Lake County
(SLCo), the governing body of the town of Alta passed a formal resolution, a copy of which is maintained
at the local government offices.

Jurisdiction Profile
Date of Incorporation
August 1970


Location and Description
The town of Alta is a small mountain community in Little Cottonwood Canyon in the Wasatch–Cache
National Forest. The town is 4.5 square miles in area and is between 7,500 and 9,500 ft. above sea level.
It is accessed via State Highway 210, a designated scenic byway. Much of Alta is public lands, part of the
Uinta–Wasatch–Cache National Forest. The Lone Peak Wilderness and Twin Peaks Wilderness Areas
are nearby. Alta is also in the Salt Lake City watershed area. The town administration recognizes the
importance of protecting natural resources and supports protection of the watershed while facilitating




Town of Alta                                                                                               1
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



nearby recreation opportunities through interpretive signs, restroom facilities, personnel, and trail
maintenance.


Population
The 2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau records the
population of the town of Alta as 337 people.


Demographics
Most of the 337 residents are between the ages of 20 and 34, with a median age of 30.2; 289 are male
(approximately 86%) and 48 are female (14%) 1. English is the primary language in 98.1% of homes, with
1.9% other Indo-European languages. 2


Brief History
Alta was founded to house miners when silver claims were staked in Little Cottonwood Canyon during the
1860s. By 1872, several thousand seasonal residents lived in the community. Economic factors and
natural disasters, including wildfire and avalanches, led to a decline in the settlement. In 1927, resident
George Watson deeded 1800 acres of his land for the development of a ski area, which opened its first lift
in 1938. The town was officially incorporated in 1970 with Lee Bronson as the first “president” of the town
for 2 years. He was elected Mayor in 1972 when the Alta Planning Commission was appointed. The town
also established an emergency dispatch center, a Marshal’s Office, and a Justice Court. A culinary water
system was added in 1978. In 1984 the Alta Fire Station was completed to house the volunteer fire
department, which is now staffed by the Unified Fire Authority (UFA). The Alta Ski Area is the centerpiece
of Alta’s economy and is one of the world’s foremost skiing destinations.


Climate
Alta fluctuates between a humid continental and a subalpine climate. Due to its high elevation, it receives
an average of 500 inches of snowfall, typically between November and May. This snowfall is influenced
by the Great Salt Lake, which can generate heavy “lake effect” snow. Average annual precipitation is
47.08 inches, predominantly occurring in the winter months. January temperatures range from an
average daily low of 15°F to an average daily high of 30.7°F. Summer temperatures are mild, with an
average low of 50.3°F and average high of 72.9°F.

Public Services
The Alta Marshal’s Office is the law enforcement agency for the town. Alta Central Dispatch provides
emergency dispatch services. Fire, EMS and HazMat response are contracted through UFA. Alta Ski
Patrol also provides first aid response to guests of the ski area.

Salt Lake County Service Area #3 (SA3) is a government water/sewer district in Little Cottonwood
Canyon at Snowbird. SA3 provides drinking water and wastewater services to Snowbird Ski Resort and
many residences along the Alta Bypass Road. It also manages the Town of Alta’s water system through
an interlocal agreement. Other partner agencies include Salt Lake County, the Utah Department of
Transportation (UDOT), the Utah Avalanche Center, Salt Lake City Public Utilities, the Salt Lake Valley
Health Department, Uinta–Wasatch–Cache National Forest Salt Lake Ranger District, Salt Lake County
Sheriff’s Office, the Cottonwood Canyons Foundation, the Central Wasatch Commission, and the Utah
Transit Authority.


Governing Body
The governing body of the town consists of a Mayor and a four-member Town Council. This council
serves as the municipal/local government, performing executive functions of different natures. Members
of this governing body are elected by the people.


Development Trends
The Town of Alta is not experiencing residential growth. The 2016 Commercial Core Plan expresses
interest in commercial development to support the creation of an identifiable Town Center to enhance
year-round commercial activity. Significant discussion regarding transportation development in Little
Cottonwood Canyon has occurred. UDOT studies of transportation demand in Little Cottonwood Canyon
have considered enhanced bus service, tolling or other restrictions on single-occupancy vehicles,
improvements in trailhead and roadside parking, and a possible gondola.


Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 3. The results are based on the criteria in Table 4 and the
equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed decisions about risk
management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to identifying and addressing
potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and proactive risk prevention. With
the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks, leading to more effective risk
management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

     R I S K F A CT O R ( R F ) E Q U A T I O N

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.


Hazard Event History
Examining hazard event histories provides valuable insights to inform decision making and help prioritize
resources for risk prevention and response efforts. For almost all hazard events, the most significant
vulnerability in the town of Alta is the potential for isolation from the rest of the Salt Lake Valley. Alta sits
at the top of Little Cottonwood Canyon—a box canyon accessible only by SR-210. With only one road
into and out of Alta (which is frequently affected by various weather conditions), the town runs the risk of
isolation from partner agencies, leaving it in standalone operations with very limited resources. The
elderly and medically fragile populations are most at risk, as there are very limited medical resources in
the town, but all residents, commuters, and visitors are affected if the supply of medical care, food, fuel,
and other essential supplies is cut-off.

The Town Manager is appointed as the floodplain administrator for Alta. The town’s Flood Damage
Prevention Ordinance was adopted 3/11/2010 and amended 4/12/2023. The current effective FIRM is
dated 9/25/2009. There is no identified Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA). Therefore, Alta does not
issue permits in the SFHA. If a SFHA were to be identified in the future, the Building Department would
be responsible for issuing permits in accordance with the specifications outlined in the Flood Damage
Prevention Ordinance. Since there is no SFHA, Alta also cannot issue substantial damage or substantial
improvement determinations given that both of these terms are applicable only to structures in the SFHA.


Jurisdiction-Specific Vulnerabilities and Impacts
Table 8 provides information on the vulnerable assets in the town of Alta, including its critical facilities,
highlighting the town’s vulnerability to identified hazards. By understanding the risks associated with
these assets, local authorities can develop proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities and ensure that
the safety and functionality of these important assets during hazard events. These data are invaluable for
decision-making and prioritizing resources for emergency response and preparedness efforts, ultimately
contributing to more effective risk management and greater resilience in the community.

Assets vulnerable in the Town of Alta include facilities such as the Town Marshal’s office, the Town EOC,
the town library, and UFA Station 113, which lies just outside of the city boundary but serves the town and
canyon areas. A one-room classroom is located within the Goldminer’s Daughter Lodge and is served by
Granite School District. Little Cottonwood Canyon Road/SR 210 is the only access road to the town and
connects it to the rest of Salt Lake County. Two ski resorts, Alta and Snowbird, and associated
businesses are significant to the economy within the town and the region. The area has many trails for
summer recreation as well. The natural resources include forest and other vegetation, Little Cottonwood
Creek and tributaries, wildlife, and the scenic appeal of the mountains.

 Dam Failure   People           Vulnerability: Alta lies downstream of Cecret Lake Dam, an earthen

                                Impacts: A sudden release of water could create flash flooding, which

                                Contaminated waters from dam failure could also spread disease.
                                Red Pine Dam inundation maps show that Little Cottonwood Canyon
                                Road would be impacted at the mouth of the canyon, which could
                                close SR-210 for an unknown period of time. This would disrupt
                                transportation into and out of Alta.
               Structures       Vulnerability: Ski area base facilities could be inundated in a

               Assets           dam failure.

                                consequences for the people in the community. Such attacks can shut

                                transportation, and utilities (water and electricity) and compromise

Jurisdiction-Specific Changes in Vulnerability

can be influenced by climate change, population patterns, and land use developments. Understanding
these factors is crucial for the town of Alta to develop a resilient community and minimize the impacts of
hazards. Table 9 displays the unique changes within the community and the related effects on each
identified hazard affecting the town of Alta.

Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing



36                                                                                                  Town of Alta
                        SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,
mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•     Regularity Capabilities

•     Administrative Capabilities

•     Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•     Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•     Attending other planning/program meetings

•     Participating in other planning processes; and

•     Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.
The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.
Regular efforts should be made to monitor the progress of mitigation actions implemented through other
planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.

Capability Assessment
Local mitigation capabilities are existing authorities, policies, programs, and resources that reduce hazard
impacts or could help carry out hazard mitigation activities.

Financial Capabilities
Financial capabilities are the resources to fund mitigation actions. Talking about funding and financial
capabilities is important to determine what kinds of projects are feasible, given their cost. Mitigation
actions like outreach programs are lower cost and often use staff time and existing budgets. Other
actions, such as earthquake retrofits, could require substantial funding from local, state, and federal
partners. Partnerships, including those willing to donate land, supplies, in-kind matches, and cash, can be
included.

Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve Capabilities
Actions that can expand and improve existing authorities, plans, policies, and resources for mitigation
include budgeting for mitigation actions, passing policies and procedures for mitigation actions, adopting



42                                                                                              Town of Alta
                      SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



and implementing stricter mitigation regulations, approving mitigation updates, and making additions to
existing plans as new needs are recognized. Table 18 lists the opportunities for the town of Alta.

Table 18: Opportunities to Expand or Improve the Capabilities of the Town of Alta

 Capability             Opportunity to Expand and/or Improve
 Planning and           • Explore adopting Wildland Urban Interface code
 Regulation             • Update vegetation management ordinance
                        • Update our development regulations pertaining to Avalanche Hazards
                        • Update wind and snow loading criteria
                        Improvement of local knowledge and capabilities will occur with ongoing
                        exploration and review of unknowns in the context of planning and regulations.
                        A culture of continuous learning and capacity building among local officials,
                        planners, and community members will occur.
                        Alta does not have any ordinances or land use regulations specifically for
                        avalanche hazards. It is beginning to implement avalanche analysis into
                        construction design, and the new Town Hall building was constructed to
                        withstand a 1% annual chance avalanche hazard. The update to Alta Ski Lifts
                        Master Plan does have considerations for avalanche mitigation. This
                        represents an important first step for the town and ski area as their current
                        methods (firing artillery shells) are becoming outdated. In addition, these
                        methods might not be available to them soon—and they are 100% dependent
                        on this method to function as a town and from an economic standpoint. The
                        town has received communication from the U.S. Department of Defense
                        informing them that they must consider alternative methods for control work,
                        as artillery will soon be unavailable.
 Administrative         • Updated GIS data
 and Technical          To address the unknowns in administrative and technical capabilities, a
                        thorough assessment of current staffing levels and expansion can be
                        considered. For the Chief Building Official, it is essential to determine if the
                        current levels are adequate. In addition, providing specialized training on
                        hazards and mitigation strategies and enhancing coordination through regular
                        interagency meetings would be beneficial. For the Civil Engineer, evaluating
                        the current workload and staffing needs is crucial. Offering targeted training
                        programs focused on hazard identification and mitigation techniques and
                        enhancing coordination through collaborative projects could improve
                        capabilities. The Community Planner’s effectiveness can be boosted by
                        assessing staffing adequacy, implementing continuous professional
                        development programs on hazard and mitigation planning, and fostering better
                        interagency coordination through joint task forces or working groups.
                        For the Emergency Manager, reviewing staffing levels, ensuring that staff are
                        trained on the latest hazard mitigation practices, and creating a centralized
                        communication system to streamline coordination are key steps. The
                        Floodplain Administrator’s capabilities can be enhanced by performing a
                        staffing review, introducing training modules covering flood hazards and
                        mitigation measures, and organizing inter-departmental workshops to improve
                        coordination. Hiring or training staff to manage GIS functions effectively,
                        facilitating training sessions on GIS tools, and establishing clear protocols and
                        regular meetings for improved coordination can strengthen the capabilities of
                        the GIS Coordinator role.
 Financial              • Pursue Grant Opportunities

SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



 Capability             Opportunity to Expand and/or Improve
                        • MOU’s with ski area and local hotels for feeding and sheltering folks in
                           emergency to have their costs covered
                        To address the unknowns in financial capabilities, several opportunities for

                        comprehensive assessment to identify existing funding resources and their

                        To address the unknowns in education and outreach capabilities, there are
                        several opportunities for improvement and expansion. First, it is essential to
                        conduct an in-depth assessment of current insurance disclosures and outreach
                        practices to understand the integration of hazard mitigation information.
                        Collaborating with insurance companies, including mitigation-related content in
                        their communications to policyholders, can increase awareness and
                        preparedness.
                        Next, identifying and engaging with organizations that represent, advocate for,
                        or interact with underserved and vulnerable communities is crucial. Partnering
                        with these organizations can help tailor hazard mitigation messages to the
                        specific needs of these communities, ensuring that critical information reaches
                        those most at risk. This collaboration can lead to the development of targeted
                        outreach programs and initiatives that effectively address the unique
                        challenges faced by these communities.
                        For social media, a comprehensive strategy should be developed to leverage
                        various platforms. This strategy should include regularly updating content,
                        engaging with the community through interactive posts, and using social media
                        analytics to measure the effectiveness of outreach efforts. Expanding the use
                        of social media to other platforms can also increase the reach and impact of
                        hazard mitigation messages.

City of Bluffdale Annex
To participate in this multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan (MJHMP) update for Salt Lake County
(SLCo), the governing body of the city of Bluffdale passed a formal resolution, a copy of which is
maintained at the local government offices.

Jurisdiction Profile
Date of Incorporation
October 13, 1978


Location and Description
The city of Bluffdale is located 20 miles south from downtown Salt Lake City in the southern portion of
Salt Lake County. The city is approximately 11.4 square miles in area and is located approximately 4,436
feet above sea level. Bluffdale is known for its suburban feel with a mix of residential neighborhoods,
open spaces, and some commercial areas. The city is bordered by the Jordan River to the west and the
Wasatch Mountains to the east providing residents with beautiful natural scenery and outdoor recreational
opportunities.




City of Bluffdale                                                                                        1
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



Population
The 2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau records the
population of the city of Bluffdale at 18,168 people.


Demographics
Most of the 18,168 people are between the ages of 35 and 44, with a median age of 31.2; 9,214 are
males (50.7%) and 8,954 are females (49.3%).

English is the primary language in 93.5% of homes, with 3.5% Spanish, 1.8% Other Ind-European
languages, 1.2% Asian and Pacific Islander languages, and less than 0.1% other languages.


Brief History
In 1862, Jens and Rise Madsen became the first permanent settlers on the east side of the Jordan River.
Chris Petersen and his family along with Timothy Gilbert and the Spencer Brothers, John and Robert
soon followed. The construction of the canal system in 1874 led to an influx of settlers. Bluffdale Precinct
was established in 1883 with William Wallace Merrill serving as the first justice of the peace. The
community began to grow with a post office being established in 1888, a meetinghouse built between
1887 and 1888, a brick schoolhouse in 1893, and an amusement hall in 1899. The arrival of the Narrow
Gauge Railroad in 1876 further connected Bluffdale to the surrounding areas. Bluffdale was officially
incorporated in October 1978.


Climate
The city of Bluffdale experiences a humid continental climate (Dfa Köppen classification). This is
characterized by hot, dry summers and cold, snowy winters. Average high temperatures are
approximately 80–90°F in the summer and in the 20s and 30s in the winter. Rain each year is
approximately 20 inches, and snowfall averages 30–40 inches.


Public Services
Because Bluffdale lies at the narrowest point between the Wasatch and Oquirrh mountain ranges, many
utilities are located here. These utilities and other critical infrastructure and key resources (CIKR)
significantly influence the city’s land uses. These include a heavily used Union Pacific Railroad and UTA
rail line running north-south; Redwood Road (also running north–south); Interstate-15 and Bangerter
Highways; and a major canal that is the effective western boundary of the community. In addition, six
other canals, several aqueducts, two major power corridors, regional arterials and highways, and a major
gas line corridor create obstacles and shape land use opportunities.

Bluffdale has an established fire department, police department, and also has emergency management,
public works, code enforcement, utilities, and building departments.




2                                                                                             City of Bluffdale
                       SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



Governing Body
The city of Bluffdale operates under a six-member council system with a governing body consisting of the
Mayor and five council members. The City Council created the position of City Manager through an
ordinance who is responsible for the daily operations and management of the city including its employees
and services. The City Manager reports directly to both the Mayor and the City Council.


Development Trends
The entire Wasatch Front is under tremendous growth pressure, with the Wasatch Front Regional Council
projecting a 67% increase in population by 2040. Bluffdale’s 2018 Capital Facilities Plan (CFP) uses a
detailed methodology to project population in connection with projected future land use in the city. Based
on the CFP, Bluffdale’s population will grow to nearly 40,000 by the year 2035. At this point, the city will
be at full build-out (given its current future land use planning and the associated dwelling densities). More
detailed information about population projections is included in the CFP document. Population growth is
expected to increase dramatically with the new housing developments presently under construction. The
major population growth center in Bluffdale will be the east side of the city, between I-15 and the railroad
tracks, where the heaviest growth is expected to occur between approximately 2015 and 2025, and then
tapering off as Bluffdale nears build-out.


Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 3. The results are based on the criteria in

Table 4 and the equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed
decisions about risk management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to
identifying and addressing potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and
proactive risk prevention. With the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks,
leading to more effective risk management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

     RISK FACTOR (RF) EQUATION

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.

The City Engineer is the designated Floodplain Administrator for the city of Bluffdale. The city’s Flood
Control Ordinance was adopted on 8/11/2009. The current effective FIRM is dated 11/19/2021. The
Building Department is responsible for permitting, including inspecting structures. All development in the

the flood zone and type of work (such as channel improvements, structural development, etc.).

improvement determinations are made through the permitting process. When the permit request is
submitted, there is the opportunity to indicate whether the structure meets these definitions prior to permit
approval and will therefore be required to come into compliance with current code.


Jurisdiction-Specific Vulnerabilities and Impacts
Table 8 provides information on the vulnerable assets in the city of Bluffdale, including its critical facilities,
highlighting the city’s vulnerability to identified hazards. It also describes the potential impacts on the
community arising from those vulnerabilities. By understanding the risks associated with these assets,
local authorities can develop proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities and ensure the safety and
functionality of these important assets during hazard events. These data are invaluable for decision-
making and prioritizing resources for emergency response and preparedness efforts, ultimately
contributing to more effective risk management and greater resilience in the community.

Vulnerable assets in Bluffdale include the population of 18,168 and their residences. Critical facilities in
Bluffdale include one EOC, two fire stations, one police station, two elementary schools, and four charter
schools. Bluffdale City Park, Wardle Fields Regional Park, and Jordan Narrows Park are some of the
primary outdoor recreation facilities, as well as the Jordan River Parkway multi-use trail. Bangerter
Highway runs along the northern border of the city, I-15 follows much of the eastern border, and Porter
Rockwell Blvd, Redwood Road, and 14600/14400 South are primary routes through the city. Although
Mountain View Corridor is not within Bluffdale, it closely parallels the southwest border and is a significant
route for the city.

of hazards. Table 9 displays the changes within the city and the related effects of each hazard on the city

Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing
methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,
mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•      Regularity Capabilities

•      Administrative Capabilities

•      Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•      Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•      Attending other planning/program meetings

•      Participating in other planning processes; and




 38                                                                                                City of Bluffdale
                       SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



•     Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.

The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.
Regular efforts should be made to monitor the progress of mitigation actions implemented through other
planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.
Table 9 lists existing planning mechanisms in which the Hazard Mitigation Plan has been integrated.
Table 13 lists the opportunities for integrating elements of this plan into other plans.

Financial Capabilities
Financial capabilities are the resources to fund mitigation actions. Talking about funding and financial
capabilities is important to determine what kinds of projects are feasible, given their cost. Mitigation
actions like outreach programs are lower cost and often use staff time and existing budgets. Other
actions, such as earthquake retrofits, could require substantial funding from local, state, and federal
partners. Partnerships, including those willing to donate land, supplies, in-kind matches, and cash, can be
included.

Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve Capabilities
Actions that can expand and improve existing authorities, plans, policies, and resources for mitigation
include budgeting for mitigation actions, passing policies and procedures for mitigation actions, adopting
and implementing stricter mitigation regulations, approving mitigation updates, and making additions to
existing plans as new needs are recognized. Table 18 lists the opportunities for the city of Bluffdale.




 44                                                                                          City of Bluffdale
                       SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN


Table 18: Opportunities to Expand or Improve the Capabilities of the City of Bluffdale

 Capability           Opportunity to Expand and/or Improve
 Planning and         Bluffdale can expand its planning and regulatory mitigation capabilities by
 Regulation           integrating the mitigation actions in this plan into the Capital Improvement Plan,
                      Economic Development Plan within the General Plan, Land Use Plan, and
                      Transportation Plan, which is in the process of being updated. Aligning these
                      planning mechanisms with the mitigation plan will increase the odds of successfully
                      implementing the identified projects.
 Administrative       Bluffdale can expand partnerships for mitigation, including identifying and acting
 and Technical        upon any deficiencies identified during a review of mutual-aid agreements and
                      memoranda of understanding (MOUs). Partnerships can help when developing
                      grant applications and project implementation through either financial or in-kind
                      support, letters of support, or time and materials. Other local governments and
                      agencies in hazard mitigation as well as nonprofits and community-based
                      organizations can be effective mitigation partners. Partners can also provide
                      technical skills, such as GIS, which Bluffdale does not have in-house. Further,
                      bringing the right partners together and establishing a Coordinating Group can
                      ensure effective communications.
 Financial            Bluffdale can apply for new grants which fund hazard mitigation actions including
                      but not limited to the Hazard Mitigation Grant Program (HMGP/404), Flood
                      Mitigation Assistance (FMA), and Public Assistance Mitigation (PA Mitigation/406).
 Education and        Bluffdale can expand current public outreach methods by developing programs to
 Outreach             target specific groups which may be at higher risk of disaster impacts or able to
                      implement hazard mitigation measures including homeowners, developers, schools,
                      and people with special needs. This may include direct training and education of
                      developers, professionals, and representatives of people with special needs.
                      Additional outreach could incorporate community leaders who are familiar with each
                      of these populations, as well as newsletters to homeowners with information on the
                      hazards that could impact their area and how they can reduce their risk such as
                      through home retrofits.

Town of Brighton Annex
To participate in this multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan (MJHMP) update for Salt Lake County
(SLCo), the governing body of the town of Brighton passed a formal resolution, a copy of which is
maintained at the local government offices.

Jurisdiction Profile
Date of Incorporation
January 1, 2020


Location and Description
The town of Brighton is a newly incorporated community located at the top of Big Cottonwood Canyon.
The town is approximately 15.9 square miles in area and is approximately 8,700 feet above sea level.
The town of Brighton is the home of the Brighton Ski Resort and the Solitude Mountain Resort. Figure 1 is
a map of the town.




Town of Brighton                                                                                         1
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN




                                    Figure 1: Map of the Town of Brighton 1


Population
The 2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau records the
population of the town of Brighton as 353 people.




1 Town of Brighton Map. https://www.brighton.utah.gov/media/2491.




2                                                                                 Town of Brighton
                      SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



Demographics
Most of the 353 people are between the ages of 25 and 34, with a median age of 43.1; 182 (51.6%) are
males and 171 (48.4%) are females. English is the primary language in 99.4% of homes,.


Brief History
The town of Brighton boasts a storied history that began in 1871 with its initial settlement by Scottish
immigrants William and Catherine Brighton who established a rustic hotel that quickly became a favored
spot for visitors enjoying the natural beauty of Big Cottonwood Canyon. In 1936, the Brighton Ski Resort
was founded, marking it as one of Utah’s earliest ski destinations. As the community grew, residents
voted to incorporate the town, with Brighton officially incorporating on January 1, 2020.


Climate
The town of Brighton experiences a continental climate (Dsa Köppen classification), characterized by dry,
hot summers and cold winters, with significant temperature variations throughout the year. Average highs
are approximately 81°F in the summer and approximately 15°F in the winter. Rain each year is
approximately 15.3 inches, and snowfall averages 500 inches.


Public Services
The town of Brighton offers a wide range of public services through the Great Salt Lake Municipal
Services District (MSD). MSD provides staffing and administrative support and other services and
handles planning and zoning, business licensing, code enforcement, inspections, and emergency
planning. Public works services are contracted with SLCo Public Works, which provides construction and
maintenance of roads, snow removal, and street lighting.


Governing Body
The governing body—Mayor and four council members—is responsible for making policy decisions,
adopting ordinances, and overseeing the administration of the town.


Development Trends
The Brighton Neighborhood Nodes Design Plan aims to increase amenities, commercial/recreational
vitality, walking facilities, and sustainability in specific areas.


Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 3. The results are based on the criteria in Table 4 and the



Town of Brighton                                                                                             3
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed decisions about risk
management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to identifying and addressing
potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and proactive risk prevention. With
the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks, leading to more effective risk
management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

     RISK FACTOR (RF) EQUATION

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.

The town of Brighton has designated the Director of Planning and Development Services as the
Floodplain Administrator. The duties of the Floodplain Administrator are supported by the Greater Salt
Lake Municipal Services District (MSD). The current Flood Damage Prevention and Control Ordinance
was adopted on 9/14/2021. The current Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) became effective 9/25/2009.
The MSD is responsible for issuing floodplain permits in MSD Member Communities, including Brighton.
The permits include a description of all work, including the kind and type of construction, proposed intent,
and location. Substantial damage/substantial improvement structures are identified through the permitting
process. Structures that are determined to be substantially damaged or substantial improvements are
required to come into compliance with current codes. The MSD Building Department provides guidance
on how to build in accordance with existing building codes.


Jurisdiction-Specific Vulnerabilities and Impacts
Table 8 provides information on the vulnerable assets in the town of Brighton, including its critical
facilities, highlighting the town’s vulnerability to identified hazards. It also describes the potential impacts
on the community arising from those vulnerabilities. By understanding the risks associated with these
assets, local authorities can develop proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities and ensure the safety
and functionality of these important assets during hazard events. These data are invaluable for decision-
making and prioritizing resources for emergency response and preparedness efforts, ultimately
contributing to more effective risk management and greater resilience within the community.

Vulnerable assets include the 353 residents and their homes. Brighton has one fire station. Highway
190/Big Cottonwood Canyon Road provides the primary transportation route in and out of Brighton. In the
summer, Guardsman Pass Road provides a transportation link to Summit County to the east. Solitude
Mountain Resort and Brighton Resort, along with associated businesses, account for significant economic
assets in the town that draw significant numbers of visitors and revenue. The area also offers summer
recreation through campgrounds and trails. Natural resources include forests and other vegetation,
wildlife, lakes, Big Cottonwood Creek and tributaries, and the general scenery of the Wasatch mountains.

Although this number deviates from the 353 residents reported by the 2020 U.S. Census, the Town of
Brighton 2025 Community Wildfire Protection Plan reports the following: 432 full-time residents, 185 full-
time housing units, 1,200 part-time residents, and 690 seasonal housing units, 875 homes, 900 buildable
lots, and 5 commercial entities.

 Radon             People          Vulnerability: In Brighton, homeowners and seasonal residents living in

                                   exposure.

                   Assets          property investors, and local business owners in Brighton.

Jurisdiction-Specific Changes in Vulnerability
Hazard events can impact communities, infrastructures, and ecosystems. The severity of these impacts
can be influenced by climate change, population patterns, and land use developments. Understanding
these factors is crucial for the town of Brighton to develop a resilient community and minimize the impacts
of hazards. Table 9 displays the changes within the town and the related effects on each hazard to the
town of Brighton.

Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing
methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,
mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•   Regularity Capabilities

•   Administrative Capabilities

•   Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•   Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•   Attending other planning/program meetings



Town of Brighton                                                                                           43
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



•     Participating in other planning processes; and

•     Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.

The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.
Regular efforts should be made to monitor the progress of mitigation actions implemented through other
planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.

Table 11 lists the opportunities for integrating elements of this plan into other plans

Financial Capabilities
Financial capabilities are the resources to fund mitigation actions. Talking about funding and financial
capabilities is important to determine what kinds of projects are feasible, given their cost. Mitigation
actions like outreach programs are lower cost and often use staff time and existing budgets. Other
actions, such as earthquake retrofits, could require substantial funding from local, state, and federal
partners. Partnerships, including those willing to donate land, supplies, in-kind matches, and cash, can be
included.

Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve Capabilities
Actions that can expand and improve existing authorities, plans, policies, and resources for mitigation
include budgeting for mitigation actions, passing policies and procedures for mitigation actions, adopting
and implementing stricter mitigation regulations, approving mitigation updates, and making additions to
existing plans as new needs are recognized. Table 18 lists the opportunities for the town of Brighton.

Table 18: Opportunities to Expand or Improve the Capabilities of the Town of Brighton

 Capability          Opportunity to Expand and/or Improve
 Planning and        Improvement of local knowledge and capabilities will occur with encourage of
 Regulations         ongoing exploration and review of unknowns in the context of planning and
                     regulations. A culture of continuous learning and capacity building among local
                     officials, planners, and community members will occur.
 Administrative      To address the unknowns in the administrative and technical capabilities table,
 and Technical       several opportunities for improvement and expansion can be considered. For the
                     Chief Building Official, it is essential to conduct a thorough staffing assessment to
                     determine if the current levels are adequate. In addition, providing specialized
                     training on hazards and mitigation strategies and enhancing coordination through
                     regular interagency meetings would be beneficial. For the Civil Engineer, evaluating
                     the current workload and staffing needs is crucial. Offering targeted training
                     programs focused on hazard identification and mitigation techniques and enhancing
                     coordination through collaborative projects could improve capabilities. The
                     Community Planner’s effectiveness can be boosted by assessing staffing
                     adequacy, implementing continuous professional development programs on hazard
                     and mitigation planning, and fostering better interagency coordination through joint
                     task forces or working groups.
                     For the Emergency Manager, reviewing staffing levels, ensuring that staff are
                     trained in the latest hazard mitigation practices, and creating a centralized
                     communication system to streamline coordination are key steps. The Floodplain
                     Administrator’s capabilities can be enhanced by performing a staffing review,
                     introducing training modules covering flood hazards and mitigation measures, and
                     organizing inter-departmental workshops to improve coordination. Hiring or training
                     staff to manage GIS functions effectively, facilitating training sessions on GIS tools,
                     and establishing clear protocols and regular meetings for improved coordination
                     can strengthen the capabilities of the GIS Coordinator role.
 Financial           To address the unknowns in financial capabilities, several opportunities for
                     improvement and expansion can be considered. It is essential to conduct a
                     comprehensive assessment to identify existing funding resources and their past
                     use. This assessment will provide a clear understanding of which resources have
                     been used for specific activities and can fund future mitigation actions.
 Education and       To address the unknowns in education and outreach capabilities, there are several
 Outreach            opportunities for improvement and expansion. First, it is essential to conduct an in-
                     depth assessment of current insurance disclosures and outreach practices to
                     understand the integration of hazard mitigation information. Collaborating with
                     insurance companies, including mitigation-related content in their communications
                     to policyholders, can increase awareness and preparedness.
                     Next, identifying and engaging with organizations that represent, advocate for, or
                     interact with underserved and vulnerable communities is crucial. Partnering with
                     these organizations can help tailor hazard mitigation messages to the specific
                     needs of these communities, ensuring that critical information reaches those most
                     at risk. This collaboration can lead to the development of targeted outreach

Canyons School District Annex
To participate in this multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan (MJHMP) update for Salt Lake County
(SLCo), the governing body of the Canyons School District submitted a commitment letter to participate in
the planning process. Upon approval from FEMA, the plan will be adopted by a formal resolution, a copy
of which will be maintained at the district offices.

Jurisdiction Profile
Location and Description
The Canyons School District is in the southeastern part of Salt Lake County. It serves the municipalities
of Alta, Cottonwood Heights, Draper, Midvale, and Sandy (see Figure 1). The district covers 192 square
miles and includes 50 schools with approximately 34,000 students. The district offers a range of
educational programs, including 29 elementary schools, eight middle schools, five traditional high
schools, and eight special programs schools. These special programs include a technical school, a
special education school, and a high school for adults in prison. Canyons School District was established
in 2007 after residents voted to split from the Jordan School District. It officially started operating on July
1, 2009.

Brief History
The Canyons School District was established in 2007 after residents in southeastern Salt Lake County
voted to split from the Jordan School District. This made Canyons the first new school district created in
the state in nearly a century. 3 The district officially began operations on July 1, 2009. David Doty, a former
high school Spanish teacher and assistant commissioner for the Utah System of Higher Education, was
appointed as the district’s first superintendent. Over the years, the district has grown to include 47
schools and approximately 34,000 students.

In 2014, James Briscoe became superintendent, and in 2020, Rick Robins took over the role. The district
continues to serve the communities of Alta, Cottonwood Heights, Draper, Midvale, and Sandy.


Climate
Salt Lake County, where Canyons School District is located, experiences a semi-arid climate
characterized by hot, dry summers and cold, snowy winters. The region typically has four seasons, with
average summer temperatures reaching the 80s to 90s°F (27–37°C). In comparison, winter temperatures
can drop into the 20s to 30s°F (-6 to 4°C). Precipitation is relatively low, mostly occurring during the
spring and early summer months. Snowfall is common in winter, contributing to the area’s overall water
supply. The surrounding mountains can influence weather patterns, leading to occasional heavy snowfall

in the winter months. The climate impacts various aspects of school life, including potential outdoor
activities and commuting conditions.


Public Services
The Canyons School District provides public services to support student education and well-being. These
include comprehensive academic programs, extracurricular activities, and specialized support for
students with diverse needs. The district offers counseling and mental health services; nutritional
programs, such as free and reduced lunch options; and opportunities for advanced placement and career
and technical education. In addition, the district emphasizes community engagement through family
support services and partnerships that enhance learning environments. These services aim to ensure that
students have the necessary resources to thrive academically and personally.


Governing Body
The governing body of the Canyons School District is the Canyons School District Board of Education,
which is responsible for setting policies, overseeing the district’s budget, and making decisions that affect
the educational programs and operations of the district.


Development Trends
The Canyons School District in Utah has experienced several notable development trends. The district is
focusing on expanding its Career and Technical Education (CTE) programs to better prepare students for
the workforce, with a significant development being the purchase of the former eBay campus in Draper
for $50 million to create the Canyons Center of Innovation. This new facility will offer classes in robotics,
engineering, business, and other technical fields.

Since its establishment in 2009, the district has rebuilt or renovated 23 schools, addressing seismic
issues and modernizing facilities to ensure safety and accommodate growing student populations.
Moreover, the district is aligning its development plans with regional economic trends and long-term
strategic goals, leveraging the location of new facilities, such as the proximity of the new Center of
Innovation to public transportation and the Point Innovation District.


Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 3. The results are based on the criteria in Table 4 and the
equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed decisions about risk
management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to identifying and addressing
potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and proactive risk prevention. With
the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks, leading to more effective risk
management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

   RISK FACTOR (RF) EQUATION

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.

National Flood Insurance Program Summary
The Canyons School District does not participate in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) or the
Community Rating System.


Jurisdiction-Specific Vulnerabilities and Impacts
Table 7 provides information on the vulnerable assets in the Canyons School District, including its critical
facilities, highlighting the district’s vulnerability to identified hazards. It also describes the potential impacts
to the community arising from those vulnerabilities. Impacts are the consequences or effects of each
hazard on the assets. By understanding the risks associated with these assets, the district can develop
proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities and ensure the safety and functionality of these important
assets during hazard events. These data are invaluable for decision-making and prioritizing resources for
emergency response and preparedness efforts, ultimately contributing to more effective risk management
and greater resilience.

Vulnerabilities include 33,493 students, 7,020 district employees, 28 elementary schools, 8 middle
schools, 6 high schools, and 5 other schools, as well as school buses, other vehicles, and other
equipment used in educational programs.

                                   Impacts: Daily school or other gatherings may be postponed or

 Tornado          People           Vulnerability: Students and staff are vulnerable to tornadoes.
                                   Tornadoes are rare but could occur anywhere in the district.
                                   Impacts: Flying debris, collapsed structures, and vehicle or bus
                                   accidents caused by high winds can lead to injuries or fatalities.
                                   Families may be temporarily or permanently displaced due to
                                   damaged homes. Student access to education may be interrupted.
                  Structures       Vulnerability: All district facilities, schools, and vehicles are vulnerable
                                   to tornado damage.
                                   Impacts: Tornadoes can damage or destroy school buildings, homes,
                                   vehicles, and businesses. Roofs can be torn off, windows shattered,
                                   and buildings leveled.
                  Economic         Vulnerability: There are vulnerabilities related to costs for district

                                   activities held at the school may be delayed or canceled.
 Wildfire         People           Vulnerability: Students and staff are vulnerable to the effects of
                                   wildfires.
                                   Impacts: Smoke and poor air quality from wildfires can affect the whole
                                   region, even if fire is not within the district. Smoke can cause
                                   respiratory issues, especially for children and those with pre-existing
                                   conditions like asthma. This may require the cancellation of outdoor
                                   events and necessitate indoor recess. Families in evacuated areas
                                   may need to leave their homes, disrupting daily life.
                  Structures       Vulnerability: No structures were identified in high wildfire risk areas.

Hazards Not Profiled
Avalanche risk has been omitted from further discussion of hazard impacts and from mitigation actions.
As shown in the description in Volume 1, avalanche risk is primarily in the Wasatch Mountains in SLCo.
CSD schools and other facilities are not located within known avalanche paths and not near slopes with
potential impact from avalanches. No previous occurrences of avalanches have impacted CSD facilities
or assets.


Jurisdiction-Specific Changes in Vulnerability
Natural hazards can have a range of specific impacts on the Canyons School District, affecting the school
environment and the broader community. The severity of these impacts can be influenced by climate
change, population patterns, and land use developments. Understanding these factors is crucial for the
Canyons School District to develop a resilient community and minimize the impacts of hazards. Table 8
lists some unique changes within the community and the related effects on each identified hazard to the
CSD.

Additional Public Involvement
The Canyon School District proactively informs students and families about potential hazards and safety
issues. The district uses a multi-faceted approach to public outreach, which includes regular
communication through newsletters, social media updates, and community meetings. It also provides
essential resources on its official website, offering guidelines on how to prepare for and respond to
various emergencies, such as natural disasters and health concerns. The school district also collaborates
with local emergency services to hold safety drills and workshops, ensuring that families are well-informed
and equipped to handle potential threats. This commitment to transparency and education helps foster a
safe and informed community for all students and their families.


Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing
methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,
mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•    Regularity Capabilities

•    Administrative Capabilities

•    Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•    Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•    Attending other planning/program meetings

•    Participating in other planning processes; and

•    Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.

The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.
Regular efforts should be made to monitor the progress of mitigation actions implemented through other
planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.
Canyons School District was not a participant in the previous mitigation plan, so it has not yet integrated
hazard mitigation into other existing plans. Table 9 lists existing planning mechanisms in which the
MJHMP has been integrated. Table 10 lists the opportunities for integrating elements of this plan into
other plans.

Capability Assessment
Local mitigation capabilities are existing authorities, policies, programs, and resources that reduce hazard
impacts or could help carry out hazard mitigation activities. School districts do not have the same
planning obligations and procedures as municipalities. As such, their capabilities will be described in a
narrative rather than the table format of the municipal annexes.


Planning and Regulatory Capabilities
Planning and regulatory capabilities are the plans, policies, codes, and ordinances that prevent and
reduce the impacts of hazards.

District Policy 300.05 – Emergencies and Safety Procedures addresses the adoption of an emergency
response plan and the district’s responsibility to assist individual schools to develop safety procedures
and a District Emergency Response Plan and to train district and school staff on the roles in the
emergency plan.

Canyons School District adheres to federal law and the building codes adopted by the State of Utah from
various international and national code organizations. The Facilities Services Department addresses
specific code questions.




Canyons School District                                                                                    31
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



Administrative and Technical Capabilities
Administrative and technical capabilities include staff and their skills. They also include tools that can help
carry out mitigation actions.

District staff includes financial and administrative services, facilities management, and employees who
specialize in coordinating with state and federal programs. The external relations department provides
efforts in public engagement. It is not known whether these departments are familiar with hazard
mitigation. There is potential to expand this capability for district departments to engage in additional
mitigation activities.


Financial Capabilities
Financial capabilities are the resources to fund mitigation actions. Talking about funding and financial
capabilities is important to determine what kinds of projects are feasible, given their cost. Mitigation
actions like outreach programs are lower cost and often use staff time and existing budgets. Other
actions, such as earthquake retrofits, could require substantial funding from local, state, and federal
partners. Partnerships, including those willing to donate land, supplies, in-kind matches, and cash, can be
included.

The financial capabilities of the Canyons School District include management of governmental and
proprietary funds. Major funds including the general fund, capital outlay fund, and debt service fund
account for 90.7% of government fund expenditures. Specific funds are as follows:


GOVERNMENTAL FUNDS
•    General Fund: including activities such student instruction, student services, staff services, district
     administration, school administration and support services, and student transportation

•    Capital Outlay Fund (a major fund): Long-term building program to construct new schools and
     renovate existing schools

•    Debt Service Fund (a major fund): General obligation bonds

•    Pass-Through Taxes Fund

•    District Activity Fund

•    Canyons Education Foundation Fund

•    Nutrition Services Fund


PROPRIETARY FUND
•    Self-insurance Fund

Education and Outreach Capabilities
Education and outreach capabilities are programs and methods that could communicate about and
encourage risk reduction. These programs may be run by a participant or a community-based partner.
Partners, especially those who work with underserved communities, can help identify additional education
and outreach capabilities.

The Canyons School District communicates with students, parents, and employees through a variety of
methods. Information is shared via the district and individual school websites, email newsletters, the
ParentSquare messaging system for email, text, and app notifications, social media, and other methods.
These communication tools provide opportunities to share information regarding potential mitigation
activities.


Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve Capabilities
Actions that can expand and improve existing authorities, plans, policies, and resources for mitigation
include budgeting for mitigation actions, passing policies and procedures for mitigation actions, adopting
and implementing stricter mitigation regulations, approving mitigation updates, and making additions to
existing plans as new needs are recognized. Table 11 lists the opportunities for the CSD to expand or
improve.

Jurisdiction Profile
Date of Incorporation
Copperton became a metro township in January 2017, then converted to a town on May 1, 2024.


Location and Description
The town of Copperton is located southwest of Salt Lake City. The town is approximately 0.3 square
miles in area and is approximately 5,400 feet above sea level. It is renowned for its picturesque
landscapes and historical importance. The Copperton Historic District, which is listed on the National
Register of Historic Places, includes over 230 contributing buildings.




Town of Copperton                                                                                        1
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



Population
The 2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau records the
population of the town of Copperton as 865 people.


Demographics
Most of the 865 people are between the ages of 25 and 34, with a median age of 32; 461 are females
(53.3%) and 404 are males (46.7%). English is the primary language in 88.4% of homes,, with 7.9%
Spanish, and 3.7% other languages.


Brief History
In 1926, Copperton was established by the Utah Copper Company as a residential area and model city
for its employees. It was designed to showcase company-subsidized family life featuring model brick and
stucco homes, a community park, and amenities like electricity and paved streets. Construction of
housing units ended in the 1930s and company-furnished housing ended in 1955. The town was added to
the National Register of Historic Places in 1986 preserving its unique history and architecture.


Climate
The town of Copperton experiences a humid subtropical climate (Cfa Köppen classification) characterized
by hot, humid summers and mild winters with consistent precipitation throughout the year. Average highs
are approximately 78°F in the summer and approximately 33°F in the winter. Annual precipitation is
approximately 16 inches annually with snowfall averaging 79 inches annually.


Public Services
The town of Copperton offers a wide range of public services through the Greater Salt Lake Municipal
Services District (MSD). The MSD provides staffing and administrative support and other services and
handles planning and zoning, business licensing, code enforcement, inspections, emergency planning,
and related municipal services. Public works services are contracted with SLCo Public Works, which
encompasses the construction and maintenance of roads, snow removal, and street lighting.


Governing Body
The town of Copperton’s governing body is the Copperton Council, which includes the Mayor, Deputy
Mayor, and three council members.


Development Trends
The community is physically separated from development in nearby communities by mining operation
buffer areas.

Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 3. The results are based on the criteria in Table 3 and the
equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed decisions about risk
management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to identifying and addressing
potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and proactive risk prevention. With
the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks, leading to more effective risk
management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

   RISK FACTOR (RF) EQUATION

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.

National Flood Insurance Program Summary
The town of Copperton participates in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). Table 6 displays
statistics related to the NFIP. The town of Copperton does not participate in the Community Rating
System.

Table 6: National Flood Insurance Program Status for the Town of Copperton 2

 Init FHBM        Init FIRM       Current Effective       Adopted         Date Joined NFIP        Tribal
 Identified       Identified      Map Date                Date
 12/18/85         12/18/85        9/25/09                 2009            6/3/20                  No

No information was available regarding active NFIP policies, coverage amounts, losses or payments for
the Town of Copperton.

Copperton has designated the Director of Planning and Development Services as the Floodplain
Administrator. The duties of the Floodplain Administrator are supported by the Greater Salt Lake
Municipal Services District (MSD). The current Flood Damage Prevention and Control Ordinance was
adopted on 10/20/2021. The current FIRM became effective 9/25/2009. The MSD is responsible for
issuing floodplain permits in MSD Member Communities, including Copperton. The permits include a
description of all work, including the kind and type of construction, proposed intent, and location.
Substantial damage/substantial improvement structures are identified through the permitting process.
Structures that are determined to be substantially damaged or substantial improvements are required to
come into compliance with current codes. The MSD Building Department provides guidance on how to
build in accordance with existing building codes.


Jurisdiction-Specific Vulnerabilities and Impacts
Table 7 provides information on the vulnerable assets in the town of Copperton, including its critical
facilities, highlighting the [town’s vulnerability to identified hazards. By understanding the risks associated
with these assets, local authorities can develop proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities and ensure
the safety and functionality of these important assets during hazard events. This data is invaluable for
decision-making and prioritizing resources for emergency response and preparedness efforts, ultimately
contributing to more effective risk management and greater resilience in the community.

Community assets that may be vulnerable to hazards in Copperton include the 865 residents, 1 fire
station, Copperton Park, and the Bingham Canyon Lions Club community center. Primary roads in
Copperton are 10200 South, SR 48 (New Bingham Hwy), and SR 209 (Old Bingham Hwy). The Rio Tinto
Kennecott copper mine is a significant industry near Copperton. It is accessed through Copperton and the
Kennecott office building is just outside the town. Natural resources in the area include the mineral
contents in the nearby hills, vegetation and wildlife in the foothills, and Bingham Creek. The Copperton
Historic District includes 237 buildings and 2 contributing structures in the town, mainly homes built for

Hazards Not Profiled
Avalanche has been omitted from further discussion of hazard impacts and from mitigation actions. As
shown in the description in Volume 1, avalanche risk is primarily in the Wasatch Mountains in SLCo. No
previous occurrences of avalanche have impacted Copperton.


Jurisdiction-Specific Changes in Vulnerability
Hazard events can impact communities, infrastructures, and ecosystems. The severity of these impacts
can be influenced by climate change, population patterns, and land use developments. Understanding
these factors is crucial for the town of Copperton to develop a resilient community and minimize the
impacts of hazards.

Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing
methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,
mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•   Regularity Capabilities

•   Administrative Capabilities

•   Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•   Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•   Attending other planning/program meetings

•   Participating in other planning processes; and

•   Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.

The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.
Regular efforts should be made to monitor the progress of mitigation actions implemented through other




Town of Copperton                                                                                          29
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.
