 and Technical       mitigation. For example, providing hazard-specific mitigation training for the Chief
                     Building Official and the Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) team.
 Financial           The city can focus on expanding mitigation grant writing capabilities, such as by
                     participating in state or federal Direct Technical Assistance programs, to be able to
                     apply and win pre- and post-disaster mitigation grants like the Hazard Mitigation
                     Grant Program (HMGP).

Jordan School District Annex
To participate in this multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan (MJHMP) update for Salt Lake County
(SLCo), the governing body of the Jordan School District passed a formal resolution, a copy of which is
maintained at the local government offices.


Planning Process Contact Information
Table 1 provides information on the point of contact during the updating of the MJHMP.

Table 1: Contact Information for the Jordan School District

 Name                                    Contact Information
 Ian Roberts                             Phone: 801-567-8885 email: ian.roberts@jordandistrict.org

The Jordan School District has a fully integrated approach to hazard mitigation planning and program
implementation. During the 2024 update process, the MJHMP participation roles in Table 2 were
recorded.

Jurisdiction Profile
Date of Incorporation
1904


Location and Description
The Jordan School District, in the southwestern part of Salt Lake County, encompasses a vibrant and
diverse community that includes several suburban neighborhoods and rural areas. Established in 1904, it
has grown to serve a large student population, making it one of the largest school districts in the state,
with 68 schools. The district prides itself on its commitment to providing a high-quality education, offering
various academic programs, extracurricular activities, and support services to meet the needs of its
students. With many elementary, middle, and high schools, the district is dedicated to fostering an
inclusive environment that promotes student achievement and well-being, making it a vital part of the
local community. Jordan School District provides educational opportunities for students living in the cities


Jordan School District                                                                                      1
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



of Bluffdale, Herriman, Riverton, South Jordan, West Jordan, and Copperton, and southwest portions of
unincorporated Salt Lake County (see Figure 1).


Population
For the 2024–2025 school year, the Jordan School District had 57,083 students enrolled. 1 Figure 2
presents the demographics of the students in the district.


Brief History
The district was established in 1904, starting with a student population 3,354. 2 Its name and initial
boundaries derived from the Jordan Stake of the LDS Church, which then stretched across the entire Salt
Lake Valley, from east to west, and extended from around Midvale to the valley’s southern end. 3


Climate
Salt Lake County experiences a semi-arid climate characterized by hot, dry summers and cold, snowy
winters. The region typically has four seasons, with average summer temperatures reaching the 80s to
90s°F (27–37°C). In comparison, winter temperatures can drop into the 20s to 30s°F (-6 to 4°C).
Precipitation is relatively low, mostly occurring during the spring and early summer months. Snowfall is
common in winter, contributing to the area’s overall water supply. The surrounding mountains can
influence weather patterns, leading to occasional heavy snowfall in the winter months. The climate can
impact various aspects of school life, including outdoor activities and commuting conditions. 4


Public Services
The Jordan School District provides public services to support student education and well-being. These
services include comprehensive academic programs, extracurricular activities, and specialized support for
students with diverse needs. The district offers counseling and mental health services; nutritional
programs, such as free and reduced lunch options; and opportunities for advanced placement and career
and technical education. In addition, the district emphasizes community engagement through family
support services and partnerships that enhance learning environments. These services aim to ensure that
students have the necessary resources to thrive academically and personally.

Governing Body
The district is overseen by the seven members of the Board of Education, elected by voters from the
district’s five precincts. Elections for the School Board take place every two years in November alongside
the general election. When new members are sworn in, they also select a president and a vice president.
The Board values public involvement, providing various opportunities for community members to
participate in decision-making through School Community Groups, ad hoc committees, task forces, and
other organizations. The Board of Education appoints both the Superintendent of Schools and the
Business Administrator, and the district operates under the general oversight of the Utah State Office of
Education. 7

The Jordan School District is poised for several development trends to enhance educational quality and
community engagement. In May 2023, the district established a new elementary school in Herriman,

Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 3. The results are based on the criteria in Table 4 and the
equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed decisions about risk
management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to identifying and addressing
potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and proactive risk prevention. With
the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks, leading to more effective risk
management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

     RISK FACTOR (RF) EQUATION

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.

Jurisdiction-Specific Vulnerabilities and Impacts
Table 6 provides information on the vulnerable assets in the Jordan School District, including its critical
facilities, highlighting the district’s vulnerability to identified hazards. By understanding the risks
associated with these assets, local authorities can develop proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities
and ensure the safety and functionality of these important assets during hazard events. These data are
invaluable for decision-making and prioritizing resources for emergency response and preparedness
efforts, ultimately contributing to more effective risk management and greater resilience in the community.

Vulnerabilities include over 57,000 children served by JSD, as well as 7,048 faculty and staff. Structures
include 42 elementary schools, 13 middle schools, 10 high schools and technical schools, and 3 special
schools. The district also maintains office buildings, school buses, and other vehicles that may be
vulnerable to loss from hazards.

Hazards Not Profiled
Avalanche has been omitted from further discussion of hazard impacts and from mitigation actions. As
shown in the description in Volume 1, avalanche risk is primarily in the Wasatch Mountains in Salt Lake
County. No JSD schools or facilities are located within known avalanche paths or near slopes where
avalanche is likely to occur. Additionally, there have been no previous occurrences of avalanches
impacting JSD facilities or assets.


Jurisdiction-Specific Changes in Vulnerability
Hazard events can impact communities, infrastructures, and ecosystems. The severity of these impacts
can be influenced by climate change, population patterns, and land use developments. Understanding
these factors is crucial for the Jordan School District to develop a resilient community and minimize the
impacts of hazards. Table 7 displays the unique changes each identified hazard has had on the Jordan
School District.

Additional Public Involvement
The Jordan School District proactively informs students and families about potential hazards and safety
issues. The district uses a multi-faceted approach to public outreach, which includes regular
communication through newsletters, social media updates, and community meetings. It also provides
essential resources on its official website, offering guidelines on preparing for and responding to various
emergencies, such as natural disasters and health concerns. In addition, the school district collaborates
with local emergency services to hold safety drills and workshops, ensuring that families are well-informed
and equipped to handle potential threats. This commitment to transparency and education helps to foster
a safe and informed community for all students and their families. Figure 3 and Figure 4 show examples
of public outreach.




                Figure 3: Facebook (left) and X (right) Posts for the Hazard Mitigation Survey

Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing
methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,
mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•   Regularity Capabilities

•   Administrative Capabilities

•   Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•   Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•   Attending other planning/program meetings

•   Participating in other planning processes; and

•   Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.

The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.

planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.

Financial Capabilities
Financial capabilities are the resources to fund mitigation actions. Talking about funding and financial
capabilities is important to determine what kinds of projects are feasible, given their cost. Mitigation
actions like outreach programs are lower cost and often use staff time and existing budgets. Other
actions, such as earthquake retrofits, could require substantial funding from local, state, and federal
partners. Partnerships, including those willing to donate land, supplies, in-kind matches, and cash, can be
included.

Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve Capabilities
Actions that can expand and improve existing authorities, plans, policies, and resources for mitigation
include budgeting for mitigation actions, passing policies and procedures for mitigation actions, adopting
and implementing stricter mitigation regulations, approving mitigation updates, and making additions to
existing plans as new needs are recognized. Table 16 lists the opportunities for the Jordan School
District.

Table 16: Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve the Capabilities of the Jordan School District

 Capability              Opportunity to Expand and/or Improve
 Planning and            The district does not develop or participate in many plans that relate to mitigation,
 Regulation              but these plans can still impact the district’s planning for its own assets. The district
                         can review the current building codes, including seismic standards, and identify
                         which schools can be upgraded in alignment with current codes.
 Administrative          The district can identify partners to help fill in gaps in capabilities, such as GIS,
 and Technical           hazard data collection, and experience with mitigation grants. SLCo is one example
                         of a partner that could help expand this type of capability, in addition to the
                         communities where the school district operates.
 Financial               The district can pursue new funding sources like the Hazard Mitigation Grant
                         Program. Additionally, the district can consider if and when BRIC is replaced to
                         assess whether the new grant is a viable opportunity for further mitigation financing.
 Education and           The district can share additional information with students, staff and faculty on
 Outreach                hazards and how to reduce their risk. For example, the district’s current ability to
                         offer handouts and host public meetings could incorporate additional hazard
                         information like regular earthquake or seasonal flood notices. Partners, such as
                         SLCo, could help identify and provide relevant information to share.

Jurisdiction Profile

Date of Incorporation
Kearns became a metro township in January 2017, then converted to a city on May 1, 2024.


Location and Description
The city of Kearns is located southwest of Salt Lake City. The city is approximately 4.6 square miles in
area and is approximately 4,500 feet above sea level. The city offers a blend of residential neighborhoods
and recreational facilities that is home to the Utah Olympic Oval, an indoor speed skating rink built for the
2002 Winter Olympics.




City of Kearns                                                                                             3
SALT LAKE COUNTY MULTI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD MITIGATION PLAN



Population
The 2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau records the
population of the city of Kearns as 37,058 people.


Demographics
Most of the 37,058 people are between the ages of 35 and 44, with a median age of 32.3; 18,666 are
females (50.4%) and 18,392 are males (49.6%). English is the primary language in 62.7% of homes,, with
32.3% Spanish, and 5% other languages.


Brief History
During World War II, the area was initially developed as the Kearns Army Air Base to serve as a critical
training facility for aircrew members. The base was decommissioned after the war, and the land was
gradually converted to a residential community. Named after Senator Thomas Kearns, the area saw
significant growth and development and became a prominent suburb of Salt Lake City. Today, Kearns is
known for its diverse population, community spirit, and notable landmarks.


Climate
The city of Kearns experiences a humid continental climate (Dfb Köppen classification) characterized by
warm summers and cold winters. Average high temperatures are approximately 85°F in the summer and
approximately 36°F in the winter. Rain each year is approximately 15.4 inches, and snowfall averages 60
inches annually.


Public Services
The city of Kearns offers a wide range of public services through the Greater Salt Lake Municipal
Services District (MSD). The MSD oversees services like planning and zoning, business licenses,
inspections, emergency planning, and other municipal services.


Governing Body
The city of Kearns governing body comprises the Mayor, Deputy Mayor, and a three-member council.


Development Trends
The Kearns General Plan, adopted in 2020 and amended in 2021 and 2022, outlines a community-driven
vision for land use, transportation, economic development, and housing, including elements on resilience,
infrastructure, and moderate-income housing. Kearns is also experiencing population growth, making it
one of the younger and more diverse municipalities in Salt Lake County. This is driving the need for more
housing and community services. Efforts are underway to boost the local economy through job creation


4                                                                                            City of Kearns
                      SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



and support for local businesses. These trends reflect Kearns’ commitment to fostering a vibrant and
sustainable community.


Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 5. The results are based on the criteria in Table 6 and the
equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed decisions about risk
management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to identifying and addressing
potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and proactive risk prevention. With
the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks, leading to more effective risk
management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

   RISK FACTOR (RF) EQUATION

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.

National Flood Insurance Program Summary
The city of Kearns participates in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). Table 8 displays statistics
related to the NFIP. The city of Kearns does not participate in the Community Rating System (CRS).

Table 8: National Flood Insurance Program Status for the City of Kearns 2

 Initial FHBM     Initial FIRM       Current Effective     Adopted          Date Joined NFIP      Tribal
 Identified       Identified         Map Date              Date
 12/18/85         12/18/85           09/25/09              2009             05/26/20              No

Table 9: National Flood Insurance Program Overview for the City of Kearns

 Community ID           Number of Losses        Total Net Payment        Active Policies     Total Coverage
 490265                          0                       $0                     1               $350,000

The city of Kearns has designated the Director of Planning and Development Services as the Floodplain
Administrator. The duties of the Floodplain Administrator are supported by the Greater Salt Lake
Municipal Services District (MSD). The current Flood Damage Prevention and Control Ordinance was
adopted on 8/9/2021. The current Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) became effective on9/25/2009. The
MSD is responsible for issuing floodplain permits in MSD Member Communities, including Kearns. The
permits include a description of all work, including the kind and type of construction, proposed intent, and
location. Substantial damage/substantial improvement structures are identified through the permitting
process. Structures that are determined to be substantially damaged or substantial improvements are
required to come into compliance with current codes. The MSD Building Department provides guidance
on how to build in accordance with existing building codes.

community arising from those vulnerabilities. By understanding the risks associated with these assets,
local authorities can develop proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities and ensure that the safety and
functionality of these important assets during hazard events. These data are invaluable for decision-

Community assets that may be vulnerable to hazards include 1 fire station, 1 police station, 11 schools,

Mountain View Corridor and Bangerter Highway, but neither directly intersect the city. Other primary
routes include 4700 South, 5400 South, 6200 South, and 5600 West. Element Event Center and the Utah
Olympic Oval are other notable facilities in the community.

Hazards Not Profiled
Avalanche and dam failure are not profiled for the City of Kearns. The terrain in Kearns is relatively level
and not conducive to avalanche, and no previous avalanches have occurred there. No high or significant
hazard dams are located in Kearns and no dam inundation boundaries intersect the city.


Jurisdiction-Specific Changes in Vulnerability
Hazard events can impact communities, infrastructures, and ecosystems. The severity of these impacts
can be influenced by climate change, population patterns, and land use developments. Understanding
these factors is crucial for the city of Kearns to develop a resilient community and minimize the impacts of
hazards.

Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing



26                                                                                               City of Kearns
                        SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,
mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•     Regularity Capabilities

•     Administrative Capabilities

•     Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•     Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•     Attending other planning/program meetings

•     Participating in other planning processes; and

•     Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.

The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.
Regular efforts should be made to monitor the progress of mitigation actions implemented through other
planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.
Table 12 lists existing planning mechanisms in which the Hazard Mitigation Plan has been integrated.
Table 13 lists the opportunities for integrating elements of this plan into other plans

impacts or could help carry out hazard mitigation activities.

Financial Capabilities
Financial capabilities are the resources to fund mitigation actions. Talking about funding and financial
capabilities is important to determine what kinds of projects are feasible, given their cost. Mitigation
actions like outreach programs are lower cost and often use staff time and existing budgets. Other
actions, such as earthquake retrofits, could require substantial funding from local, state, and federal
partners. Partnerships, including those willing to donate land, supplies, in-kind matches, and cash, can be
included.

Magna City Annex
To participate in this multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan (MJHMP) update for Salt Lake County
(SLCo), the governing body of Magna City passed a formal resolution, a copy of which is maintained at
the local government offices.


Planning Process Contact Information
Table 1 provides information on the point of contact during the updating of the MJHMP.

Magna City has a fully integrated approach to hazard mitigation planning and program implementation.
During the 2024 update process, the MJHMP participation roles in Table 2 were recorded.

 Name                      Title                             Jurisdiction
 Madison Warner            Municipal Emergency Planner       Unified Fire Authority/Salt Lake County

Jurisdiction Profile
Date of Incorporation
Magna became a metro township in January 2017 then converted to a city on May 1, 2024.


Location and Description
Magna City is located southwest of Salt Lake City. The city is approximately 37.4 square miles in area
and is approximately 4,250 feet above sea level. The city’s development has been significantly influenced
by its historical connection to the copper mining industry. The city maintains a small town appeal with
notable landmarks, such as the Empress Theatre and Please Green Cemetery, that reflect Magna’s rich
history.


Population
The 2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau records the
population of Magna City as 29,488 people.

Magna City                                                                                               1
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



Demographics
Most of the 1,465 people are between the ages of 35 and 34, with a median age of 32.5; 15,239 are
males (51.7%) and 14,249 are females (48.3%). English is the primary language in 71.3% of homes,, with
23.7% Spanish, and 5% other languages.


Brief History
Magna City has a rich history rooted in the mining industry. Founded in the early 1900s, Magna quickly
became known for its copper mining and processing as it became a community for workers of the Utah
Copper Company. The city’s name is derived from the Latin word meaning “great” or “large,” reflecting the
significant copper deposits found in the area. As mining operations expanded, Magna City attracted a
diverse population seeking employment opportunities. The city has preserved its historical heritage, and
today Magna City offers a blend of historical charm and modern amenities.


Climate
Magna City experiences a cold semi-arid climate (Bsk Köppen classification) characterized by hot, dry
summers and cold winters with moderate precipitation. Average high temperatures are approximately
92°F in the summer and approximately 23°F in the winter. Rain each year is approximately 15.4 inches,
and snowfall averaged 52 inches.


Public Services
Magna City offers a wide range of public services through the Greater Salt Lake Municipal Services
District (MSD). The MSD provides staffing and administrative support and other services and handles
planning and zoning, business licensing, code enforcement, inspections, emergency planning, and
related municipal services. Public works services are contracted with SLCo Public Works, which
encompasses the construction and maintenance of roads, snow removal, and street lighting.


Governing Body
The Magna City governing body consists of a Mayor and City Council, and it has an appointed City
Manager.


Development Trends
The city recently approved its first General Plan since incorporating as a metro township in 2017. This
plan guides the future of planning and development in Magna, focusing on key elements, such as land
use, transportation, housing, economic development, parks, trails, recreation, open space, natural
hazards, community facilities, and sustainability. Magna converted from a metro township to a city on May
1, 2024.

Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 3. The results are based on the criteria in

Table 4 and the equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed
decisions about risk management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to
identifying and addressing potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and
proactive risk prevention. With the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks,
leading to more effective risk management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

   RISK FACTOR (RF) EQUATION

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.

National Flood Insurance Program Summary
Magna City participates in the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). Table 6 displays statistics
related to the NFIP. Magna City does not participate in the Community Rating System (CRS).

Table 7: National Flood Insurance Policies for Magna City

    Community ID      Number of Losses        Total Net Payment       Active Policies     Total Coverage
    490266            0                       $0                      1                   $350,000

Magna City has designated the Director of Planning and Development Services as the Floodplain
Administrator. The duties of the Floodplain Administrator are supported by the Greater Salt Lake
Municipal Services District (MSD). The current Floodplain Hazard Regulations were adopted on
6/16/2023. The current Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) is dated 9/25/2009. The MSD is responsible for
issuing floodplain development permits in MSD Member Communities, including Magna City. The permits
include a description of all work, including the type of construction, proposed intent, and location.
Substantial damage/substantial improvement structures are identified through the permitting process and
through utilizing FEMA’s Substantial Improvement/Substantial Damage Desk Reference. Structures that
are determined to be substantially damaged or substantially improved are required to come into
compliance with current codes. The MSD Building Department provides guidance on how to build in
accordance with existing building codes.



1 FIRM = Flood Insurance Rate Map, FHBM = Flood Hazard Boundary Map

Jurisdiction-Specific Vulnerabilities and Impacts
Table 8 provides information on the vulnerable assets in Magna City, including its critical facilities,
highlighting the city’s vulnerability to identified hazards. It also describes the potential impacts to the
community arising from those vulnerabilities. By understanding the risks associated with these assets,
local authorities can develop proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities and ensure the safety and
functionality of these important assets during hazard events. This data is invaluable for decision-making
and prioritizing resources for emergency response and preparedness efforts, ultimately contributing to
more effective risk management and greater resilience in the community.

Critical facilities in Magna include two fire stations, one police station, and seven schools. Other
community facilities include the Magna Library, Magna Senior Center, Magna Fitness & Recreation
Center, and Kennecott-Magna Pool. Parks include Great Salt Lake State Park, Magna Copper Park,
Magna Regional Park, Pleasant Green Park, Copper Club Golf Course, and several other neighborhood
parks. Primary transportation routes include Highway 201, I-80, Highway 111/8400 West, and 3500
South. The Empress Theater, Magna Community Baptist Church, Great Saltair, and Magna Commercial
Downtown Historic District are notable historic sites in the city.

Jurisdiction-Specific Changes in Vulnerability
Hazard events can impact communities, infrastructures, and ecosystems. The severity of these impacts
can be influenced by climate change, population patterns, and land use developments. Understanding
these factors is crucial for Magna City to develop a resilient community and minimize the impacts of
hazards. Table 9 displays the changes within the city and the related effects of each hazard on Magna

Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing
methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,
mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•      Regularity Capabilities

•      Administrative Capabilities

•      Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•      Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•      Attending other planning/program meetings

•      Participating in other planning processes; and

•      Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.


28                                                                                                     Magna City
                      SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.
Regular efforts should be made to monitor the progress of mitigation actions implemented through other
planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.

Financial Capabilities
Financial capabilities are the resources to fund mitigation actions. Talking about funding and financial
capabilities is important to determine what kinds of projects are feasible, given their cost. Mitigation
actions like outreach programs are lower cost and often use staff time and existing budgets. Other
actions, such as earthquake retrofits, could require substantial funding from local, state, and federal
partners. Partnerships, including those willing to donate land, supplies, in-kind matches, and cash, can be
included.

Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve Capabilities
Actions that can expand and improve existing authorities, plans, policies, and resources for mitigation
include budgeting for mitigation actions, passing policies and procedures for mitigation actions, adopting
and implementing stricter mitigation regulations, approving mitigation updates, and making additions to
existing plans as new needs are recognized. Table 18 lists the opportunities for Magna City.

Table 18: Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve the Capabilities of Magna City 5

 Capability           Opportunity to Expand and/or Improve
 Planning and         Magna became a city on May 1, 2024, and must now build out a city leadership
 Regulation           team. All services are currently contracted out to UPD, UFA, or the MSD/Salt Lake
                      County. As it moves forward, it must decide whether it wants to continue those
                      contracts or start its own. For example, the city can review the MSD’s CEMP and
                      Stormwater Management Plan to ensure they include all local data and procedures,
                      updating them as needed.
 Administrative       Staff could receive additional training on hazards and mitigation, including building
 and Technical        officials, engineers, planners, emergency management, floodplain management,
                      and GIS personnel. Additionally, coordination between the MSD and Magna can be
                      expanded to ensure thorough understanding and implementation of mitigation
                      measures and related plans, policies, and programs.
 Financial            Magna could apply for new grant programs, including HMA grants and NRCS
                      programs.
 Education and        Current education and outreach programs are typically conducted by SLCo, MSD,
 Outreach             and the UFA. Developing and implementing hazard-specific public education
                      programs on disaster awareness and mitigation at the local level would expand
                      Magna City’s education and outreach capabilities.

City of Midvale Annex
To participate in this multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan (MJHMP) update for Salt Lake County
(SLCo), the governing body of the city of Midvale passed a formal resolution, a copy of which is
maintained at the local government offices.


Planning Process Contact Information
Table 1 provides information on the point of contact during the updating of the MJHMP.

Table 1: Contact Information for the City of Midvale

 Name                          Contact Information
 Matt Dahl                     Phone: 801-567-7262; email: mdahl@midvaleut.gov

The city of Midvale has a fully integrated approach to hazard mitigation planning and program
implementation. During the 2024 update process, the MJHMP participation roles in Table 2 were
recorded.

Table 2: Participant List for the City of Midvale

 Name                             Title                                 Jurisdiction

Jurisdiction Profile
Date of Incorporation
1909.


Location and Description
The city of Midvale is located south of Salt Lake City in the middle of the Salt Lake Urbanized
Metropolitan Area, comprising the Wasatch Front. It is just 12 miles south of downtown Salt Lake City and
some 20 miles from four mountain resorts. The city is approximately 5.9 square miles in area and has an
elevation of 4,383 feet. The city of Midvale is known for its historical significance, especially its role in the
Mormon migration of the 19th century.




City of Midvale                                                                                               1
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



Population
The 2020 U.S. Census records the population of the city of Midvale as 36,028 people.


Demographics
According to the U.S. Census Bureau, 48.8% of the population is female. Individuals under the age of 18
make up 21.8% of the population, while 9.4% are 65 years or older. The population is composed of
70.2% White and 17.5% Hispanic residents.


Brief History
In the early 1870s and 1900s, the establishment of smelters at Bingham Junction marked a significant
development in Midvale’s history, driven by the burgeoning mining activities in nearby canyons. These
smelters processed ores from Bingham Canyon and other mines, transforming the area into an industrial
hub. The influx of industry spurred the growth of hotels, boarding houses, saloons, schools, and other
establishments, making the city’s Old Town a vibrant community center.

The smelting operations continued until 1958, when the last facility ceased operations. This closure led to
a period of economic contraction for Midvale. However, since the early 2000s, the city has experienced
remarkable growth, in part due to the redevelopment of the former smelting sites. These areas have been
transformed into thriving commercial and residential zones, contributing to Midvale’s revitalization and
economic resurgence.

Today, Midvale stands as a testament to resilience and adaptability, evolving from its industrial roots into
a dynamic city with a rich heritage and a promising future.


Climate
According to data from Weather Spark, average high temperatures for the summer range from 78°F to
86°F and the winter average low temperatures are around 27°F. Rain each year is approximately 13.7
inches, and snowfall averages 12.5 inches.


Public Services
Midvale participates in several strategic partnerships for community services. The Unified Fire Authority
(UFA) provides fire, EMS, and emergency management services. The Unified Police Department (UPD)
provides law enforcement, and Salt Lake County Animal Services addresses concerns for animal welfare
and safety. The city’s Public Works Department provides many other essential functions.

Midvale City launched the Community Building Community Initiative in 1998 to address critical health and
social challenges, growing from a small dental chair in City Hall to a 3,000-square-foot facility near the
7200 South transit stop. Since becoming a 501(c)(3) nonprofit in 2014, dedicated volunteers and
supporters have helped expand its impact, particularly within the Hispanic/Latino community across the
Salt Lake Valley and Summit County.

Governing Body
The city of Midvale’s governing body consists of a mayor and five-member City Council, and it has the
power to create and enforce laws including the authority to levy taxes.


Development Trends
Midvale City is over 100 years old but has experienced hundreds of millions of dollars in new investment
in the past few years. In the 5.9 square miles of Midvale, there is a lot of activity. It is home to a growing
population of approximately 36,028 residents and some 1,300 businesses. There are many retailers who
take advantage of the city’s strategic location with its unparalleled access to the regional transportation
system and established trade areas. It is home to many top-performing locations, mom and pop shops,
and one-of-a-kind locations.


Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 3. The results are based on the criteria in Table 4 and the
equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed decisions about risk
management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to identifying and addressing
potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and proactive risk prevention. With
the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks, leading to more effective risk
management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

     RISK FACTOR (RF) EQUATION

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.

Jurisdiction-Specific Vulnerabilities and Impacts
Table 8 provides information on the vulnerable assets in the city of Midvale, including its critical facilities,
highlighting the city’s vulnerability to identified hazards. It also describes the potential impacts to the
community arising from those vulnerabilities. By understanding the risks associated with these assets,
local authorities can develop proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities and ensure the safety and
functionality of these important assets during hazard events. This data is invaluable for decision-making
and prioritizing resources for emergency response and preparedness efforts, ultimately contributing to
more effective risk management and greater resilience in the community.

Community assets at risk include critical facilities such as two fire stations, one police station, one
emergency operations center, and nine schools. The Midvale Senior Center, Ruth Vine Tyler Library, and
Copperview Community Center are other important facilities in the community. The Salt Lake County
Public Works Complex, Sanitation Building & Shop, and Fleet, Sanitation, and Operations facilities are
located in Midvale. Midvale City Park, Union Park, Bingham Junction Park, Midvale Museum and the
Jordan River Parkway Trail are among the recreation assets in the city. Major transportation routes
include I-15, I-215, 7200 South/Fort Union Boulevard, State Street/US 89, Bingham Junction Boulevard,
900 East, and Union Park Avenue. The city is served by Utah Transit Authority Trax Red and Blue lines.
The city has invested in revitalizing historic Main Street as Midvale Main Arts and Culture District to
increase pedestrian traffic, support businesses, and improve aesthetic appeal with murals. The Connie
Crosby Family Resource Center, operated by the Road Home, serves families experiencing
homelessness in Salt Lake County.

can be influenced by climate change, population patterns, and land use development. Understanding
these factors is crucial for the city of Midvale to develop a resilient community and minimize the impacts
of hazards. Table 9 displays the unique changes within the community and the related effects on each
identified hazard affecting the city of Midvale.

                  crises. In addition, climate-        patterns.
                  driven population
                  displacement can heighten
                  tensions in receiving areas,
                  raising the risk of domestic
                  terrorism. Law enforcement’s
                  focus on climate-related
                  challenges can also limit its
                  capacity to address terrorism
                  threats. Ultimately, while
                  climate change may not
                  directly cause terrorism, its
                  effects can create an
                  environment conducive to
                  extremist activities.

Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing
methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,


36                                                                                                     City of Midvale
                        SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•     Regularity Capabilities

•     Administrative Capabilities

•     Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•     Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•     Attending other planning/program meetings

•     Participating in other planning processes; and

•     Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.
The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.
Regular efforts should be made to monitor the progress of mitigation actions implemented through other
planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.

Financial Capabilities
Financial capabilities are the resources to fund mitigation actions. Talking about funding and financial
capabilities is important to determine what kinds of projects are feasible, given their cost. Mitigation
actions like outreach programs are lower cost and often use staff time and existing budgets. Other
actions, such as earthquake retrofits, could require substantial funding from local, state, and federal
partners. Partnerships, including those willing to donate land, supplies, in-kind matches, and cash, can be
included.

Actions that can expand and improve existing authorities, plans, policies, and resources for mitigation
include budgeting for mitigation actions, passing policies and procedures for mitigation actions, adopting
and implementing stricter mitigation regulations, approving mitigation updates, and making additions to
existing plans as new needs are recognized. Table 18 lists the opportunities for the city of Midvale.

 and Technical       mitigation measures, such as through presentations on hazard mitigation, plan
                     maintenance, and mitigation projects.

Jurisdiction Profile
Date of Incorporation
December 28, 2016


Location and Description
The City of Millcreek is a residential community adjacent to Salt Lake City. The city is 12.7 square miles in
area and is approximately 4,285 feet above sea level. Situated along the Mill Creek Canyon in the Uinta–
Wasatch–Cache National Forest, Millcreek offers an abundance of outdoor recreational activities
including miles of hiking trails.


Population
The 2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau records the
population of the city of Millcreek as 63,380 people.


Demographics
Most of the 63,520 people are between the ages of 25-34, with a median age of 37.1; 32,003 are females
(50.4%) and 31,517 are males (49.6%). English is the primary language in 78.6% of homes,, with 9.7%
Spanish, and 11.7% other languages.




City of Millcreek                                                                                          3
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



Brief History
Pioneers began settling the Canyon Rim and East Mill Creek areas in the Salt Lake Valley in the mid-
1800s. By the 20th century, residential and commercial development began in Millcreek. Manufacturing
operations and summer homes of the affluent from Salt Lake City also emerged along Mill Creek,
particularly what is now known as Evergreen Avenue. Millcreek underwent a wave of growth and
transformation during this time. Between the 1930s and 1960s, suburban expansion accelerated,
exacerbated by Millcreek’s proximity to Salt Lake City, the Wasatch Mountains, and key transportation
routes. Millcreek became an attractive location for new starter home subdivisions with many veterans
taking advantage of the location after World War II and the Korean War. Development continued
throughout the 20th century and into the 21st with a focus on infill projects and smaller subdivisions. The
area near I-15 became an industrial and commercial hub that benefited from its access to major highways
and railroads. Salt Lake County experienced rapid growth from 2010 onward, prompting Millcreek
residents to push for incorporation to better manage the expansion. In 2015, voters approved the creation
of a municipal government and Millcreek was incorporated.


Climate
The City of Millcreek experiences a semi-arid climate with hot, dry summers and snowy winters.
Millcreek’s climate is impacted by the surrounding terrain, which affects both the temperature of the city
and the precipitation patterns due to the proximity to the Wasatch Mountains. Summer temperatures can
surpass 90°F, and winter temperatures range from 30°F to 40°F. The city of Millcreek experiences
significant precipitation, with snowfall ranging from 40 to 50 inches and rainfall ranging from 20 to 30
inches each year.


Public Services
The city of Millcreek offers a variety of public services to enhance the quality of life for its residents. These
services include essential utility services, such as power (Rocky Mountain Power), gas (Dominion
Energy), water (Salt Lake City Public Utilities and the Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District), sewer
(Mt. Olympus Improvement District), and solid waste management (Wasatch Front Waste & Recycling).
The Public Works Department focuses on improving infrastructure, such as roads, sidewalks, and
stormwater systems; handling snow removal; issuing permits, and ensuring that construction sites comply
with city codes. The city of Millcreek also provides various community services, including parks, trails,
recreation, and open space maintenance, along with resources for residents to report concerns and
request inspections.


Governing Body
The governing body for the City of Millcreek consists of a Mayor and a four-member city council. The city
council serves as the city government performing executive functions of different natures. Members of this
governing body are elected by the people.

Development Trends
The City of Millcreek adopted its first General Plan as of 2019, a major step forward in guiding the
development of the city. Through conversations with the Millcreek community, seven vision themes for
future development were identified: unique neighborhoods, vibrant gathering places, a thriving economy,
great connections, health and environment, the outdoor lifestyle, and enhanced culture.


Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 5. The results are based on the criteria in Table 6 and the
equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed decisions about risk
management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to identifying and addressing
potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and proactive risk prevention. With
the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks, leading to more effective risk
management and, ultimately, better outcomes.

   RISK FACTOR (RF) EQUATION

RF Value = [(Probability x 0.30) + (Spatial Extent x 0.10) + (Severity of Life/Property Impact x 0.30) +
(Warning Time x 0.10) + (Duration x 0.10) + (Response Capacity x 0.10)]


Hazards with an RF value greater than or equal to 2.5 are considered high risk. Those with RF values of
2.0 to 2.4 are considered moderate risk hazards, and those with an RF value less than 2.0 are considered
low risk. The highest possible RF value is 4.

(CRS).

 490231               3                         $20,627.98               131                  $39,395,000

The city of Millcreek has designated the City Engineer as the Floodplain Administrator. The current Flood
Damage Prevention Ordinance was adopted on 11/8/2021. The ordinance includes a freeboard
requirement of 1 foot, meaning that the lowest flood floor must be built 1 foot above the base flood
elevation. The current effective Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) date is 11/19/2021. In addition to the
current effective FIRM, Millcreek provides information on the new maps that are being developed for the
Neff’s Creek area. Millcreek also requires building permits, which are issued by the Building Department.
Both the Building Permit application and the Engineering Review Checklist for projects include multiple
opportunities to evaluate flood risk. Substantial damage/substantial improvement determinations are
made through the permitting process. Structures that meet this requirement will be required to come into
compliance with current codes, including the freeboard requirement.


Jurisdiction-Specific Vulnerabilities and Impacts
Table 10 provides information on the vulnerable assets in the city of Millcreek, including its critical
facilities, highlighting the city’s vulnerability to identified hazards. It also describes the potential impacts on
the community arising from those vulnerabilities. Impacts are the consequences or effects of each hazard
on the assets. By understanding the risks associated with these assets, local authorities can develop
proactive strategies to mitigate vulnerabilities and ensure the safety and functionality of these important
assets during hazard events. These data are invaluable for decision-making and prioritizing resources for
emergency response and preparedness efforts, ultimately contributing to more effective risk management
and greater resilience in the community.

                               the Wasatch Fault traverses Millcreek City, and a moderate to large-
                               scale earthquake could cause very strong or severe ground shaking.
                               Impacts: People could be injured or killed from objects falling or being
                               trapped in collapsed structures. The most vulnerable populations
                               include the elderly, people with disabilities, and low-income residents
                               who may lack resources to adequately prepare for or respond during
                               an emergency.
              Structures       Vulnerability: All structures in Millcreek are vulnerable to earthquakes.
                               Older buildings and homes built before modern seismic codes are
                               particularly vulnerable.
                               Impacts: Structures not built to withstand seismic events, such as
                               unreinforced masonry buildings, are at risk of significant damage or
                               collapse during an earthquake. Moderate to high liquefaction potential
                               in the western area of the city may increase the vulnerability to
                               structural damage following an earthquake.
              Economic         Vulnerability: All businesses in Millcreek are vulnerable to
              Assets           earthquakes.
                               Impacts: Earthquakes are likely to cause extensive economic losses.
                               Businesses throughout the city could experience damage to their
                               buildings and inventory. Damage to infrastructure can also disrupt the
                               ability of businesses to remain in operation. Roads, rail transit lines,
                               and utilities such as power, water, and communication systems are all
                               vulnerable to damage from earthquakes, which disrupts economic
                               activity. Earthquakes can disrupt businesses, damage commercial
                               properties, and cause a loss of revenue for the city. Damage to
                               infrastructure, such as roads and utility lines, could hinder economic
                               recovery by delaying repairs and disrupting daily operations. Repair
                               and recovery could be costly and may take months or years.

 Dam Failure   People           Vulnerability: One high hazard and two significant hazard dams are
                                located within Millcreek. In addition, Millcreek is vulnerable to dam
                                failure from dams upstream. A small area of northern Millcreek is
                                within the inundation boundary for Little Dell Reservoir. Southern
                                portions of Millcreek could be affected by dam failure at Lake Mary-
                                Phoebe or Twin Lakes dams in Big Cottonwood Canyon. All residents
                                within dam inundation boundaries are at risk.
                                Impacts: Dam failure from high hazard dams indicates immediate
                                danger to life due to sudden flooding, particularly for those living
                                downstream of dams. Residents are at risk of injury or displacement
                                from flooding caused by significant hazard dams.
               Structures       Vulnerability: Potentially hundreds of structures, including homes and
                                businesses, are located within dam failure inundation boundaries and
                                are at risk of damage in Millcreek.
                                Impacts: Homes and businesses downstream face destruction from
                                rapid flooding. Millcreek is vulnerable to failure from significant hazard
                                dams, meaning these dams have the potential to cause damage to
                                structures and infrastructure if they were to fail.
               Economic         Vulnerability: Businesses in dam inundation boundaries are vulnerable
               Assets           to dam failure.
                                Impacts: Flooded commercial properties can lead to prolonged
                                business interruptions, revenue losses, and costly rebuilding.
               Natural,         Vulnerability: Plants and habitat are vulnerable to dam failure.
               Historic, and    Impacts: Dam failure can result in catastrophic flooding, disrupting
               Cultural         ecosystems and potentially destroying habitats. Soil, trees, and other
               Resources        plants, particularly in riparian areas, can be washed away.
               Critical         Vulnerability: Roads, bridges, and utilities in the path of floodwaters
               Facilities and   might be damaged or completely fail.
               Infrastructure   Impacts: The I-215/I-80 interchange near Parley’s Canyon is within the
                                inundation boundary for Little Dell Reservoir and could be damaged.

Plan Integration
Incorporating the underlying principles of the Hazard Mitigation Plan and its recommendations into other
plans is a highly effective and low-cost way to expand their influence. All plan participants will use existing
methods and programs to implement hazard mitigation actions where possible. As previously stated,
mitigation is most successful when it is incorporated into the day-to-day functions and priorities of
government and public service. This plan builds on the momentum developed through previous and
related planning efforts and mitigation programs, and it recommends implementing actions where
possible through these other program mechanisms. These existing mechanisms include the following:

•    Regularity Capabilities

•    Administrative Capabilities

•    Fiscal Capabilities

Respective planning stakeholders will conduct implementation and incorporation into existing planning
mechanisms and will be done through the routine actions of:

•    Monitoring other planning/program agendas

•    Attending other planning/program meetings


36                                                                                               City of Millcreek
                       SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



•     Participating in other planning processes; and

•     Monitoring community budget meetings for other community program opportunities.

The successful implementation of this plan will require constant and vigilant review of existing plans and
programs for coordination and multi-objective opportunities that promote a safe, sustainable community.
Regular efforts should be made to monitor the progress of mitigation actions implemented through other
planning mechanisms. Where appropriate, priority actions should be incorporated into planning updates.

Financial Capabilities
Financial capabilities are the resources to fund mitigation actions. Talking about funding and financial
capabilities is important to determine what kinds of projects are feasible, given their cost. Mitigation
actions like outreach programs are lower cost and often use staff time and existing budgets. Other
actions, such as earthquake retrofits, could require substantial funding from local, state, and federal
partners. Partnerships, including those willing to donate land, supplies, in-kind matches, and cash, can be
included.

Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve Capabilities
Actions that can expand and improve existing authorities, plans, policies, and resources for mitigation
include budgeting for mitigation actions, passing policies and procedures for mitigation actions, adopting
and implementing stricter mitigation regulations, approving mitigation updates, and making additions to
existing plans as new needs are recognized. Table 20 lists the opportunities for the city of Millcreek.

Table 20: Opportunities to Expand and/or Improve the Capabilities of the City of Millcreek

 Capability          Opportunity to Expand and/or Improve
 Planning and        The updated General Plan can incorporate additional information from the updated
 Regulation          hazard mitigation plan, such as on risks, vulnerabilities, and actions. Plan alignment
                     can also help ensure future development takes hazard risk into consideration.
                     Additionally, the city can create a more detailed Substantial Damage Plan that
                     includes identifying the tools and data sources that should be used to make
                     substantial damage determination, guidelines for notifying property owners, and a
                     framework for integrating this information into stormwater management and land
                     use planning strategies.
 Administrative      Millcreek can identify and implement a procedure for collecting current hazard data,
 and Technical       such as records of previous disaster events and impacts. This information can be




42                                                                                           City of Millcreek
                       SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



 Capability           Opportunity to Expand and/or Improve
                      used to justify additional mitigation projects and assess losses avoided, as well as
                      enhance the next hazard mitigation plan update.
 Financial            The city has had limited success with pre-disaster mitigation funding, such as the
                      Building Resilient Infrastructure & Communities (BRIC) and Flood Mitigation
                      Assistance (FMA) grant programs. The city should consider additional opportunities
                      for pre-disaster mitigation and expanding this mitigation funding capability. For
                      example, the city could be supported through a state or FEMA-led technical
                      assistance program.
 Education and        The city could utilize the city council meetings to share key messages regarding
 Outreach             mitigation. Additional direct outreach could be conducted through workshops on
                      hazards, including workshops for vulnerable populations, such as seniors.
                      Furthermore, the city could develop an emergency management listserv through
                      which mitigation information could be shared. Additionally, the city can pursue
                      opportunities to engage real estate and development professionals to ensure they
                      are supporting disclosure of risks in high-risk areas and encouraging mitigation.

Mitigation Success Story
Neffs Canyon Emergency Facilities & Flood Mitigation Improvement project is a coordinated effort led by
Millcreek, the U.S. Forest Service, Utah Division of Emergency Management (DEM), Salt Lake County
Flood Control, including support from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the
Mount Olympus community, to reduce flood risk, improve wildfire response, and enhance public safety in
the Neffs Creek area. 5 Neffs Creek is located on an active alluvial fan that is subject to sudden and
unpredictable flooding. This risk has increased over time due to development, erosion, severe storms,
and wildfire damage. Flooding in 2019 and a wildfire event in 2020 highlighted the risks in this area. A
floodplain mapping study was completed in 2016 and was discussed among the collaborating jurisdictions
from 2016 to 2019, resulting in a new preliminary FIRM. This has implications for property owners now
categorized within newly established flood zones. Additionally, Unified Fire Authority (UFA) Station 112 is
located within the floodplain and cannot be upgraded or modernized. Addressing the flood hazard will
allow UFA to upgrade Station 112 to expand capabilities for wildfire response and other emergencies.

Phase One includes parking lot improvements to facilitate emergency vehicle access and a helicopter
pad and water well to support wildfire response in the mountains on the east side of Salt Lake County, not
just Neffs Canyon. Construction is expected to start in the summer of 2025.

Phase Two involves the construction of a below-natural-grade debris basin featuring a stormwater outlet
pipe. The proposed basin will be situated near the mouth of the canyon to collect debris, sediment, and

5 Neffs Canyon Emergency Facilities Improvement. “Project Purpose.” https://millcreekut.gov/584/Neffs-Canyon-

Emergency-Facilities-Improv



City of Millcreek                                                                                               51
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



floodwater from the canyon’s catchment area. The design will allow the water to flow through the basin
and into a new storm drainpipe below local roads back to Neffs Creek. Millcreek was awarded a
Legislative Pre-Disaster Mitigation grant to complete the geotechnical investigation, environmental
documents, and design phase of the debris basin. The city was awarded a FEMA Flood Mitigation
Assistance (FMA) grant to fund the construction of the project. Phase Two is expected to take place in
2026.

Jurisdiction Profile
Date of Incorporation
January 3, 1903


Location and Description
Situated in the heart of Salt Lake Valley, Murray spans 12.32 square miles. It is bordered by Taylorsvile,
Millcreek, Holladay, Midvale, and Cottonwood Heights. The area now incorporated as Murray City has
been occupied continuously since 1848. Explosive growth occurred after the 1870 construction of the
valley’s first smelter. Murray’s central location in the larger metropolitan area makes it important for the
city to be aware of its regional context. Regional issues such as growth, transportation, the economy,
natural resources, air quality, and open space all impact the quality of life of Murray and provide the city
with many opportunities.




City of Murray                                                                                             1
SAL T L AKE COU NTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONAL HAZARD M ITIGATION PLAN



Population
The 2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimate from the U.S. Census Bureau records the
population of the city of Murray as 49,904 people.


Demographics
Most of the 49,904 people are between the ages of 25 and 34, with a median age of 38.2; 25,051 are
males (50.2%) and 24,853 are females (49.8%). English is the primary language in 84.4% of homes,, with
7.7% Spanish, and 7.9% other languages.


Brief History
Mormon pioneers arrived in the Salt Lake Valley in 1847, and in the fall of 1848, the Mississippi Saints
followed, establishing a dispersed settlement in the southern part of the valley. This area was known by
various names, such as Mississippi Ward, Cottonwood, Big Cottonwood, and South Cottonwood.
Historical records indicate that by the 1860s, at least 20 families resided in the South Cottonwood area.
The region remained largely agricultural until 1869, when ore was discovered in Park City and Little
Cottonwood Canyon. Due to the city’s central location and railroad access, the first smelter in the region
was constructed in the city of Murray in 1870, leading to the establishment of some of the largest smelters
over the next 30 years. That same year, the South Cottonwood Post Office was established. The area
evolved with the expansion of the railroad, increased smelting activity, the establishment of the territorial
road (later known as State Street), and the development of trolley transportation. A business district
began to form along the transportation corridor. The post office, and subsequently the city, officially
changed its name from South Cottonwood to Murray in 1883, in honor of territorial governor and Civil War
general, Eli Murray.


Climate
The city of Murray experiences a humid continental climate (Dfb Köppen classification) characterized by
warm summers and cold winters with constant precipitation throughout the year. Average high
temperatures are approximately 85°F in the summer and approximately 18°F in the winter. Rain each
year is approximately 20.9 inches, and snowfall averages 22 inches.


Public Services
Over the years, the city of Murray’s crews have responded to various disasters, including riverbank
flooding, trees being toppled by microburst winds, and other weather-related hazards. Three separate
entities in the city provide drinking water: Murray City, the Jordan Valley Water Conservancy District
(JVWCD), and Salt Lake City Public Utilities (SLCPU). The city of Murray’s water system generally serves
areas west of 900 East and relies primarily on well water, which accounts for about 84 percent of the
annual demand for system water. Water in the city of Murray’s service area is supplied by eight springs
and nineteen wells, each dependent on pumps and motors to deliver water to the distribution system. The
city has emergency standby power generation at six locations and five tanks or reservoirs with a



2                                                                                               City of Murray
                      SAL T L AKE COUNTY M UL TI-JURISDICTIONA L HAZARD MITIGATION PL AN



combined storage capacity of 12 million gallons for operating and emergency storage. In emergencies,
the city of Murray has an exchange agreement with SLCPU to provide water. The JVWCD and SLCPU
water systems generally supply areas east of 900 East and provide retail delivery only, with no water
sources in the city of Murray.

Murray City Power is unique in Salt Lake County as the only municipally owned power system. Murray
City Power operates the power system in a 9.9 square mile service area, comprising 206 miles of
transmission and distribution lines, and serving approximately 14,000 residential and 3,000 commercial
customers. The system load peaks at just over 100 MW in the summer and 60 MW in the winter. To
ensure a reliable energy supply, even during disasters, the city of Murray installed three generators at the
central substation with a generating capacity of approximately 39 MW. These generators are used as a
peaking resource during summer months and remain idle until needed. In emergencies, they can provide
power to necessary areas as long as the natural gas supply is available. Fire Station 81 was rebuilt and
opened in early 2020.


Governing Body
The city of Murray originally established a Mayor–Council form of government. In 1911, state legislation
changed the government structure for first and second class cities in Utah from the Council form to the
Commission form. This change was reversed in 1981, when the city of Murray re-adopted the Mayor–
Council form of government, featuring an elected Mayor and five City Council members. To ensure
staggered terms, elections are held every two years for half of the Council members, each serving a four-
year term.


Development Trends
As the hub of Salt Lake County, the city of Murray provides a strong foundation for flourishing businesses.
The community boasts robust medical, transportation, retail/professional office, educational, and
community services, creating an ideal environment for businesses. The city is home to Intermountain
Medical Center, the largest facility of the Intermountain Healthcare system in the state. In addition,
Fashion Place Mall, a premier shopping destination, significantly contributes to sales tax revenue. The
loss of either of these employers would displace thousands of employees and create a substantial loss of
sales tax revenue.

The city of Murray has seen significant growth in both housing and commercial development. This growth
is partly due to the city’s proximity to light rail transportation and freeway access, the appeal of its medical
services community, and an excellent school district. Known for being a safe, close-knit, and friendly
community, the city of Murray is an attractive place to raise a family. However, land in the city is becoming
scarce due to land-locked boundaries, limiting future development to infill construction and redevelopment
of underutilized areas. Recent zoning changes encourage mixed-use projects and increased building
heights in certain commercial zones. Remodeling efforts are underway throughout the city, including the
rebuilding/remodeling of Fashion Place Mall and the ongoing renovations at Intermountain Medical
Center, which are expected to continue for at least the next five years.

Jurisdiction-Specific Hazards and Risk
The Calculated Priority Risk Index (CPRI) is a comprehensive assessment tool for evaluating and
prioritizing risks in a given context. It considers various factors, such as probability, impact, and urgency,
to determine the level of risk associated with events or situations. The results for each hazard, including
its risk factor (RF) value, are shown in Table 3. The results are based on the criteria in Table 4 and the
equation that follows it. The CPRI helps organizations and individuals make informed decisions about risk
management and mitigation strategies. It provides a systematic approach to identifying and addressing
potential issues, allowing for a more efficient allocation of resources and proactive risk prevention. With
the CPRI, stakeholders can prioritize their focus on the most critical risks, leading to more effective risk
management and, ultimately, better outcomes.
